newsitem.title: USA: Schwab admits mistakes with institutions.
newsitem.headline: Schwab admits mistakes with institutions.

text.p: ORLANDO, Fla., Nov 11, Reuter - Top Charles Schwab & Co Inc executives on Wednesday acknowledged past mistakes in working with its institutional, fee-based investment advisors and that big-name brokerage firms were mounting formidable competition to wrest away investor assets.

David Pottruck, Schwab president, said that, while the company emphasized its retail brokerage business, the company has "created some confusion with our Schwab institutional clients (and) we have not communicated, as well as we might have."
Pottruck and other Schwab executives spoke at the opening session of a three-day conference here for its independent institutional investment advisors.

Seeking to head off any further problems with institutional clients, Pottruck asked: "So what could unravel it? The only thing I can think of is that our partnership deteriorates, that we lose faith in one another, that we let someone else divide us, and that we consequently lose in the marketplace." The annual conference was part pep-rally and also an attempt by the company to get imput from advisors on ways to help them capture new business.
Schwab executives singled out an aggressive marketing campaigns from a variety of competitors, including giant mutual fund firms, full-service brokerages, banks and insurance companies.
The biggest current threat is with brokerage giants, especially Merrill Lynch & Co Inc, Travelers Group's Smith Barney unit and American Express Co.
"No doubt they will be making some inroads," said Charles Schwab, chairman of the financial service firm. "We will not be complacent."
The three firms have been seeking to grab investor assets by repackaging themselves as financial advisors rather than full-commission brokers, Schwab asserted.

"(They) take our customers because as they are moving toward us, we fail to continue to innovate, to change, to improve, to grow, to work together with the conviction of common purpose," Pottruck said.
"Their potential as competitors is formidable," he added. "But they are not the real thing. They are only a poor copy."
The independent investment advisors at the conference use Schwab for transaction services and to sell Schwab products.

Schwab executives divided individual investors into three categories: self-directed, or individuals who do not need financial advice; "delegators, who want to have minimal involvement in their investment decisions; and "the middle...who want to manage money themselves, but need a little help."
Schwab executive said they were especially targeting the middle market for asset growth.

Company executives estimated at $13.3 trillion the total market for U.S. investible assets. About $5 trillion was with full-service brokerages and about $760 billion was with fee- based investment advisors. Schwab projects about $74 billion in mutual fund assets in 1996, with total client assets currently at $230 billion. Schwab said that its new customer accounts have grown to about one million new accounts this year, up from 400,000 in 1987.
Pottruck said that while "our attrition is among the lowest in the brokerage industry," Schwab lost almost 1,000 customer accounts worth $1 million or more, a loss of $1 billion in assets.
